seo.title: Karmic tail 12 16 13 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Tower, Death
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 16 13 compatibility: why The Hanged Man, The Tower and Death speak not of disaster but of a couple's past, read through Joyce's “The Dead”.

title: Karmic tail 12-16-13 in compatibility: the night the past spoke up
short: In compatibility, karmic tail 12-16-13 is built from three cards people are taught to fear: The Hanged Man, The Tower, Death. Its best double in literature is James Joyce's story “The Dead”, in which nobody dies all evening. This tail is not about disaster but about the past two people bring into their union: first the couple lives in a shared “not yet”, then one day the past is spoken aloud and breaks the familiar order, and the main task is to let what came before truly end and to go on together.

sections.h2: A story in which nobody dies
paragraphs: “The Dead” is the last and longest story in Joyce's collection “Dubliners”. He wrote it in Trieste in 1907; the book came out in 1914. All of it fits into one snowy night. Two elderly sisters, the Misses Morkan, give their annual dance. Their favourite nephew, Gabriel Conroy, carves the goose, makes the after-dinner speech and sees that everything goes as it should. His wife Gretta is with him.

Near the end of the evening someone upstairs sings an old Irish song. Gretta stands still on the stairs and listens. That night, in a hotel room, she tells her husband something he had not known in all their years of marriage. As a girl in Galway she was loved by a boy, Michael Furey, who used to sing that song. The night before she left, already ill, he came through the rain into the garden below her window, and a week later he died — he was seventeen. Gretta falls asleep in tears, and Gabriel lies awake watching the snow fall outside.

The title promises death, yet nobody dies all evening. The dead here are the remembered: the boy from Galway, Gabriel's late mother, an old aunt who he thinks will soon be “a shade”. Death in the couple's tail 12-16-13 works the same way. It stands as the main task not as an event that has to happen, but as a way of relating to what has already ended.

The story runs in the order of the cards. First the pause: a husband who has looked after his wife for years, put off the important words and waited for the right moment — The Hanged Man. Then a song the tenor refused to sing all evening, and one sentence after which the night cannot be undone — The Tower. At the end an old version of the marriage quietly ends: jealousy of the dead boy goes, and for the first time Gabriel sees his wife whole, past included — Death. Joyce is quoted in the original.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man at the entry: “No, it was not the moment yet”
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, their shared wishes and common language. The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. For a 12-16-13 couple the entry is The Hanged Man, and their common language is the pause.

Gabriel has taken a room at the Gresham for one night so as not to travel home to Monkstown after the dance. At the hotel door he feels that he and his wife “had escaped from their lives and duties, escaped from home and friends” and run away to a new adventure. There it is, this couple's shared wish, though nobody says it aloud: to break out of the round of duties together. In the room Gretta walks towards him along the shaft of light from the street lamp, her face serious and weary, and the words will not pass his lips: “No, it was not the moment yet.” He talks about something else and thinks: “If she would only turn to him or come to him of her own accord!” Two people love each other and hang in suspense, each waiting for the other to take the first step.

The pause has an everyday face — care. Gabriel forces his daughter to eat her stirabout, gets green shades for his son's eyes at night and buys his wife goloshes, and his solicitude has long been a standing joke in the family. In Lisovskaya's description, The Hanged Man in a couple looks exactly like this: one does everything for the other and almost nothing for themselves. The card has a shadow too: what people will say, and what parents will say, matters more. Gabriel's mother opposed his marriage and once called Gretta “country cute”. Yet it was Gretta who nursed her mother-in-law to the very end, in their house at Monkstown. A silent sacrifice on one side, a slight remembered for years on the other.

The truest scene of The Hanged Man is the staircase. Gabriel stands in the dark hall and looks up at his wife, who has stopped at the banisters to listen. He asks himself what “a woman standing on the stairs in the shadow, listening to distant music” is a symbol of. If he were a painter he would paint her in that attitude and call the picture “Distant Music”. The Hanged Man is the card of another angle of view. Here two people look at the same evening from different sides, each suspended at their own point. He invents a title for her instead of asking what she hears.

The numbers explain where this pause comes from. The couple's entry 12 is made from the entries of two people: The Moon (18) of one and The World (21) of the other, 18 + 21 = 39 → 3 + 9 = 12. Waite calls The Moon “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”. In his list of meanings for The World stand “voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”. One brings night memory into the couple, the other a habit of leaving. In Joyce you can see it literally. Gretta has Galway, rain and a song. Gabriel has the continent: every year he goes on a cycling tour to France, Belgium or Germany, and when someone at the dance reproaches him for not knowing his own country, he snaps: “I'm sick of my own country, sick of it!” The common language of such a couple is made of two “not here”s. In the story The Moon belongs to the wife and The World to the husband; in a living couple it can be the other way round — gender decides nothing here.

sections.h2: The Tower in the middle: a song nobody meant to sing
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task (this is our reading: Lisovskaya gives the point no meaning of its own, it only adds to the main one). For a 12-16-13 couple the middle is The Tower, and it is made from The Lovers (6) of one partner and The Wheel of Fortune (10) of the other. The Lovers is the card of choice. The Wheel is a turn no one controls. The Tower is born where an old choice meets a turn of the wheel.

In Joyce the old choice is a night in her grandmother's garden, when Gretta implored a sick boy to go home and he said he did not want to live. The turn of the wheel is the tenor Bartell D'Arcy. All evening he refused to sing because of a cold — “I'm as hoarse as a crow” — and he sang only when the guests were already leaving, uncertain both of his words and of his voice. The song is “The Lass of Aughrim”, an Irish form of an old ballad that stands as number 76 in Francis Child's collection. In it a woman with a baby stands in the rain at her lover's door, and his mother will not let her in: “O, the rain falls on my heavy locks / And the dew wets my skin, / My babe lies cold…” It looks like chance. But Waite writes that behind the symbol of the Wheel lies “the denial of chance”. For the couple this means the chance song turns out to be an old choice coming back.

After that The Tower works fast. Gabriel expects tenderness and hears: “O, I am thinking about that song.” A few lines later comes the sentence after which the evening cannot be undone: “I think he died for me.” On his way to the bed Gabriel passes the cheval-glass and sees himself in full length. “While he had been full of memories of their secret life together, full of tenderness and joy and desire, she had been comparing him in her mind with another.” He sees himself as “a ludicrous figure”: a pennyboy for his aunts, a nervous, well-meaning sentimentalist orating to vulgarians — “the pitiable fatuous fellow he had caught a glimpse of in the mirror”.

Joyce himself gave such moments a name. In his draft novel “Stephen Hero” the hero calls an epiphany “a sudden spiritual manifestation”, whether in the vulgarity of speech or of gesture or in a memorable phase of the mind itself. Benebell Wen, describing The Tower's lightning, uses the same word: the card promises “a sudden epiphany, realization”. This couple's Tower is not a catastrophe but an epiphany: the minute when the past is spoken aloud and the picture each of them kept in their head stops working. Lisovskaya's tasks for The Tower include both “the collapse of an invented image of the partner” and the habit of “looking in different directions” at a hard moment. Joyce says it in almost the same words: Gretta looks away “along the shaft of light towards the window”, and Gabriel turns his back to the light lest she see the shame burning on his forehead.

In ordinary life such an evening is rarely loud. An old song in a taxi, a photograph from a box, a letter found during a move, a name dropped at the table. And suddenly one of the two realises that all this time they have lived beside a person with a separate story, and in that story they are not the hero. The first impulse is to cross-examine. Gabriel starts just like that: “Perhaps that was why you wanted to go to Galway with that Ivors girl?” Joyce calls the tone “cold interrogation”. Yet in Lisovskaya the same Tower, in its strong form, means firm support and calm in an unexpected blow. And Gabriel changes the course of the night with one decision: “He did not question her again for he felt that she would tell him of herself.” He strokes her hand and listens.

There is a clue in the numbers too. If the couple lived by the personal formula, the middle would come from the ends: 12 + 13 = 25 → 7, The Chariot. Waite calls The Chariot “above all things triumph in the mind”. Gabriel was waiting for a triumph: Joyce writes that a vague terror seized him “at that hour when he had hoped to triumph”. But the couple's middle is made not from its ends but from the middles of the two people. Instead of The Chariot's triumph, the couple has The Tower.

sections.h2: Death as the main task: the journey westward
paragraphs: A couple's main task is read mostly through its minus: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn. For tail 12-16-13 it is Death. It is made from The Lovers (6) of one partner and The Chariot (7) of the other: a choice plus a movement that cannot be turned back. In Lisovskaya, Death's tasks in a couple are to help each other separate from parents and move house, to accept a partner utterly unlike the previous one, to live through partings and distance, to see one's own mistakes and not only the other's. “The Dead” shows these tasks as scenes.

Separating from the parental home. As a girl, Gretta left her grandmother's house on Nuns' Island for the convent in Dublin. That very night, while packing, she heard gravel thrown against the window. Gabriel still carries his late mother's phrase and the role of the favourite nephew, the one whose presence makes Aunt Kate “always feel easier in my mind”.

Accepting a partner unlike the previous one. Michael Furey is a boy from the gasworks who sang and stood in the rain by the wall “where there was a tree”. Gabriel is a teacher and reviewer with gilt-rimmed glasses and goloshes, carrying a quotation from Browning he is afraid to use in case it is “above the heads of his hearers”. At first Gabriel tries to beat the difference with irony: “What was he?” — “He was in the gasworks.” The irony fails and he feels humiliated.

Seeing one's own mistakes. The mirror does this work for Gabriel before he has time to blame his wife. And then the main thing happens. “It hardly pained him now to think how poor a part he, her husband, had played in her life.” He watches Gretta asleep “as though he and she had never lived together as man and wife”, and “a strange, friendly pity for her entered his soul”. “He had never felt like that himself towards any woman but he knew that such a feeling must be love.”

What dies that night is not a person but the old Gabriel: “His own identity was fading out into a grey impalpable world.” A version of the marriage dies in which the wife had no past and the husband was the only hero of her story. Wen writes of Death as the end of one stage and the beginning of a new one, and of how people resist change. Waite calls it “change, transformation and passage from lower to higher”.

Before supper Gretta had begged: “O, do go, Gabriel. I'd love to see Galway again.” He answered coldly: “You can go if you like.” The last paragraph of the story says: “The time had come for him to set out on his journey westward.” Readers have argued for over a century about what that journey means — death, reconciliation with Ireland, or simply the trip he turned down at the dance. For the couple the meaning is simpler. The main task of tail 12-16-13 is a journey to where the partner came from: to their town, their people, their past. Not erasing that past and not competing with it, but visiting it. In the final lines the snow falls equally “upon all the living and the dead”: past and present end up under one sky and stop fighting for room.

Death as a main task has a minus too, and Joyce gave it an exact word. In a letter to his publisher Grant Richards of 5 May 1906 he explained that he had chosen Dublin as the scene of the book because the city seemed to him “the centre of paralysis”. The Misses Morkan's dance, the story says in its opening lines, had never once “fallen flat”: the same guests every year, the same goose, the same speech. Death's minus is not an ending but the impossibility of one. The couple lives in the same scene for years, and the past in it does not die but stands beside them like a third person. Jealousy of someone who is gone, comparison with those who came before, projecting their features onto the present partner — all of these are ways of not letting the past end.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre: scales between two people
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the shared atmosphere, what happens between two people away from view. Every couple with tail 12-16-13 has Justice (8) at the centre. This is not statistics but arithmetic: the partner with tail 18-6-6 always has The Hanged Man (12) at the personal centre, the partner with tail 21-10-7 always has Temperance (14), and 12 + 14 = 26 → 8. Wen tells these cards apart like this: “The theme of Justice is external balance”, while Temperance “indicates internal balance”. The couple's atmosphere is made from one partner's pause and the other's inner measure, and scales appear in it.

In Lisovskaya, Justice in a couple means honesty, faithfulness, “a cool head and a warm heart”, duties fairly shared. In its minus it is the habit of measuring everything by oneself, idealising the partner, responsibility that turns into control. Its tasks are to admit one's own fault instead of blaming, and to forgive.

In Joyce even the first kiss in the room starts with a fair account. Gabriel tells her that Freddy Malins has paid back the sovereign he lent him, though he never expected it, and Gretta kisses her husband: “You are a very generous person, Gabriel.” Half an hour later the scales tip. It turns out she had been “comparing him in her mind with another”, and he himself starts weighing what part he has played in her life. And at the end the same word, generous, comes back, this time about himself: “Generous tears filled Gabriel's eyes.” Justice at the centre of the couple begins with keeping accounts and can end in generosity.

In his after-dinner speech Gabriel jokes: “I will not attempt to play tonight the part that Paris played on another occasion. I will not attempt to choose between them.” He is speaking of the three hostesses of the dance, but he means the mythical judge who gave the apple to one of three goddesses, which began the Trojan War. At the table Gabriel refuses to judge. That same night he becomes both judge and accused.

In describing Justice, Waite separates two kinds of justice. The first is the moral principle “which deals unto every man according to his works”. The second is like the gifts of the poet: “we have them or have not”, and their presence is as much a mystery as their absence. Gabriel can show his works: care, a hotel room, goloshes. Michael Furey showed one thing: he stood in the rain. This couple's scales learn to tell what can be weighed from what cannot. The Roman jurist Ulpian defined justice as the constant will “to render to each his due”. That includes the partner's past.
The cards on our site have their own designs. This section is about the Rider–Waite–Smith deck that Waite and Wen wrote about, and in it the partners' cards literally show through the couple's cards.

ul: **The Moon on Death's horizon.** Waite writes that on the Death card, between two pillars on the verge of the horizon, “there shines the sun of immortality”. Wen specifies that these are the two pillars from The Moon. The Moon is one partner's entry (18). Their night memory stands on the horizon of the couple's main task, and the sun rises exactly there.

**The World in The Hanged Man's legs.** Wen notes that The Hanged Man's crossed legs reappear on The World and concludes: “it is the hanged man who shall attain the fulfillment of the World card”. The World is the other partner's entry (21). The couple's shared entry, The Hanged Man, carries that partner's gesture.

**The serpent on The Lovers and on the Wheel.** Waite himself describes the serpent twining round the Tree of Knowledge behind the woman on The Lovers, and Typhon in his serpent form on The Wheel of Fortune. Wen brings the two cards together: the serpent warns of “an unanticipated turn of events”, of “how quickly bliss can become tragedy”. The couple's Tower is made from one partner's Lovers and the other's Wheel.

**The living tree.** Waite's Hanged Man hangs on “living wood, with leaves thereon”. Michael Furey, in Gretta's story, stands “at the end of the wall where there was a tree”, and in Gabriel's last vision he is “a young man standing under a dripping tree”. The sacrifice Gretta speaks of stands under a tree, like The Hanged Man.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a choice made again
paragraphs: “The couple's values” is what the union exists for. In 93.5% of couples with tail 12-16-13 that place holds The Lovers (6), in 6.5% The Devil (15). The Lovers also appear in one partner's personal tail, and twice: 18-6-6. The card of choice that one person carries in their own tail almost always rises into the couple's values.

Waite recalls that the old Lovers card showed married life and was called Simulacrum fidei, “the symbol of conjugal faith”. Wen insists that “in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice”, not mere romance. For a 12-16-13 couple choice is not a “yes” said once. Gretta once chose to leave Galway and stay in Dublin. That night Gabriel chooses his wife together with her past. Faithfulness here means not pretending the past does not exist. For couples with The Devil in their values the same question is harsher: what holds the union together — a choice, or an attachment neither can step away from.

sections.h2: Nora and Jim: a story Joyce knew from inside
paragraphs: Joyce did not invent Michael Furey. His wife, Nora Barnacle, came from Galway. Before she met Joyce, two young men she had loved died there. Michael Feeney died as a teenager. Michael “Sonny” Bodkin died of consumption in February 1900 and is buried in Rahoon cemetery outside Galway. Biographers see both of them in Furey.

Joyce met Nora in Dublin on 10 June 1904, and their first walk out together fell on 16 June — the very day into which “Ulysses” would later be packed. In the autumn of 1904 they left Ireland together, unmarried. They lived as husband and wife for twenty-seven years and married only on 4 July 1931, at the Kensington register office in London — in the words biographers quote, “for testamentary reasons”: so that their children's right to inherit would be beyond dispute. Lisovskaya writes of The Hanged Man in a couple that such couples enter a relationship slowly and need a push from outside to marry. For the Joyces the push was the law — Justice, which stands at the centre of every 12-16-13 couple.

In 1912 Nora took her husband to Bodkin's grave. A year later, in Trieste, Joyce wrote the poem “She Weeps over Rahoon” in the voice of a woman weeping over the grave of “my dark lover”: “Rain on Rahoon falls softly, softly falling…” It almost exactly repeats the rhythm of the ending of “The Dead”, where the snow is “softly falling”. A husband lent his own voice to his wife's dead love. Death as a main task, lived in its plus, looks exactly like this: someone else's past is neither erased nor defeated; it is given a place.

sections.h2: How tail 12-16-13 is built: an example with 04.07.1975 and 18.12.1975
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices; if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added. The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers; it is the sum of the partners' middles.

For a person born on 04.07.1975: day 4, month 7, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task 4 + 7 + 22 = 33 → 6, centre 4 + 7 + 22 + 6 = 39 → 12, entry 6 + 12 = 18, middle 6 + 18 = 24 → 6. Personal tail 18-6-6.
For a person born on 18.12.1975: day 18, month 12, year 22. Main task 18 + 12 + 22 = 52 → 7, centre 18 + 12 + 22 + 7 = 59 → 14, entry 7 + 14 = 21, middle 7 + 21 = 28 → 10. Personal tail 21-10-7.
The couple's centre: 12 + 14 = 26 → 8, Justice. The couple's values for these two dates are The Lovers (6).
What else a search through all dates shows:

ul: **Rarity.** Tail 12-16-13 occurs in about one couple in 2,367 (0.042%): 91st place out of 97 couple tails.
**One road.** It comes from only one meeting of personal tails: 18-6-6 and 21-10-7, in 100% of such couples. That is why all of them have Justice at the centre.
**Born in the couple.** Neither The Tower nor Death appears in either partner's tail or centre: these two cards arise only through the sum.

**Never in one person.** In a personal matrix the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 13 an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre. Besides, by the personal formula the middle would be 12 + 13 → 7, while the couple has 16.
**No twins.** There are no other couple tails made of 12, 16 and 13: these three cards meet only in this order.

paragraphs: A tail shows a task, not a fate. Here is what moves a 12-16-13 couple from minus to plus.

ul: **Say the pause out loud.** “Not yet” works for one evening, not for many years. A wish each is waiting for the other to guess is better named by the one who has it.
**Ask, don't cross-examine.** When the past is spoken, the first impulse is irony and keeping score. Gabriel's night changes when he falls silent and lets his wife tell her story.
**Don't compete with someone who is gone.** A partner's past has no future, so it is no rival. It is easy to lose to it and impossible to win.
**Separate parents' voices from your own.** “Country cute” is the mother's phrase, not the husband's. In this couple other people's judgements live longer than they should.
**Go west.** Literally — to where the partner comes from, to their people and places. And figuratively — into their past, without jealousy.
**Keep the scales honest.** Justice at the centre is not about counting who gave more, but about everyone receiving their due, the past included.

paragraphs: The strong version of tail 12-16-13 is a couple that has already lived through its night after the dance. It knows how to wait but does not hide in waiting. It knows each of them had a life before they met and is not afraid to talk about it. Its evenings do not repeat one script year after year. The past in such a couple lies, like Joyce's snow, on everyone equally — and keeps no one from going on.

ul: **12 · The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is the pause: looking after each other, putting off the important words and waiting for the other to come of their own accord.
**16 · The Tower — middle of the task.** One day the past of one of the two is spoken aloud — in a song, a letter, a phrase at the table — and an evening that seemed familiar collapses in a minute.
**13 · Death — main task.** Not a loss but an ending: letting go of jealousy towards what came before, separating from parents' voices and accepting that the partner had a life before they met.

faq.q: Is karmic tail 12-16-13 a bad sign for a couple's compatibility?
faq.a: No. The Hanged Man, The Tower and Death sound frightening, but a couple's tail shows the tasks of the union, not its outcome. The numbers predict nothing: no break-ups, no misfortunes, no dates. They describe where the couple gets stuck — in the pause, in keeping score, in jealousy of the past — and where it can grow.

faq.q: Does Death as the main task mean one partner will leave?
faq.a: No. In a couple's tail Death is the end of an old form, not an event involving people: separating from parents, moving house, accepting the partner's past, letting go of an old image of the union. As in Joyce's “The Dead”, where nobody dies all evening and only an old version of a marriage comes to an end.

faq.q: Why does tail 12-16-13 never occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 13 an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre. The couple's middle is built differently too: it is the sum of the partners' middles (6 + 10 = 16), not of the ends, which would give 12 + 13 → 7.

faq.q: How can you tell whether a couple has tail 12-16-13?
faq.a: It occurs only when one partner has personal tail 18-6-6 and the other 21-10-7. Then the couple's entry is 18 + 21 → 12, the middle 6 + 10 = 16, the main task 6 + 7 = 13, and Justice is always at the centre. Example: the dates 04.07.1975 and 18.12.1975; for your own dates the compatibility calculator does the sum.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails, 12, 16 and 13 come together only in the order 12-16-13: The Hanged Man at the entry, The Tower in the middle and Death as the main task. No other sequence of these three cards occurs in compatibility.

report: The Hanged Man, The Tower and Death in a row read like a verdict. But tail 12-16-13 has a double in literature — James Joyce's story “The Dead”, in which nobody dies all evening. The dead there are the remembered. This tail works the same way: it is not about disaster but about the past two people bring into their union.

The plot fits into one snowy night in Dublin. Gabriel Conroy and his wife Gretta are at his aunts' annual dance. Near the end of the evening someone upstairs sings an old song, Gretta stands still on the stairs, and that night in the hotel she tells her husband something he had not known in all their years of marriage: as a girl in Galway she was loved by a boy who used to sing that song and died at seventeen. The story runs exactly in the order of the cards: a pause, a blow, an ending. Joyce is quoted in the original.

report.h3: “No, it was not the moment yet”

report: The entry to the task is the couple's common language, what the two want together. For a couple with this tail the entry is The Hanged Man, and their common language is the pause. Gabriel has taken a room for one night, and at the hotel door he feels that he and his wife “had escaped from their lives and duties”. But when Gretta comes towards him, the words will not come: **“No, it was not the moment yet.”** He talks about something else and thinks: “If she would only turn to him or come to him of her own accord!” Two people love each other and hang in suspense, each waiting for the other to take the first step.

The pause has an everyday face — care. Gabriel forces his daughter to eat her stirabout and buys his wife goloshes, and the whole family laughs at his solicitude. It has a shadow too: the parents' voice. Gabriel's mother opposed the marriage and called Gretta “country cute”, yet it was Gretta who nursed her to the very end. The truest scene is the staircase. Gabriel looks up at his wife, standing still, and thinks he would call such a picture “Distant Music”. He invents a title for her instead of asking what she hears.

This couple's entry is made from one partner's Moon and the other's World. Waite calls The Moon “life of the imagination”; among the meanings of The World he lists “voyage, emigration, flight”. Gretta has Galway, rain and a song; Gabriel has cycling tours on the continent and “I'm sick of my own country!”. Their common language is made of two “not here”s.

report.h3: A song the tenor never meant to sing

report: The Tower in the middle comes from one partner's Lovers and the other's Wheel of Fortune: an old choice meets a turn of the wheel. The old choice is the night Gretta implored a sick boy to go home out of the rain. The turn of the wheel is a tenor who refused to sing all evening because of a cold and sang only when the guests were already leaving. It looks like chance. But in Waite, behind the Wheel lies **“the denial of chance”**: the chance song turns out to be an old choice coming back.

After that one sentence decides everything: “I think he died for me.” Gabriel passes the mirror, sees himself in full length and understands that while he was full of tenderness, “she had been comparing him in her mind with another”. Joyce called such moments an epiphany — “a sudden spiritual manifestation”. Wen, describing The Tower's lightning, uses the same word. This couple's Tower is not a catastrophe but an epiphany: the past is spoken aloud, and the picture each of them kept in their head stops working.

The first impulse is to cross-examine. “Perhaps that was why you wanted to go to Galway?” Gabriel asks, in a tone Joyce calls “cold interrogation”. Then he changes the course of the night with one decision: **“He did not question her again for he felt that she would tell him of herself.”**

At the centre of such a couple stands Justice — scales. Even the first kiss in the room begins with a fair account: Gabriel says an acquaintance has paid back a loan, and Gretta tells him: “You are a very generous person.” Half an hour later the scales tip, and he starts weighing what part he has played in her life. Waite separates the justice that “deals unto every man according to his works” from gifts that “we have them or have not”. Gabriel can show his works: care, a hotel room, goloshes. The boy from Galway showed one thing: he stood in the rain. This couple's scales learn to tell what can be weighed from what cannot.

The main task is Death, and it is an ending, not a loss. What dies is not a person but the old Gabriel and an old version of the marriage, in which the wife had no past. “It hardly pained him now to think how poor a part he, her husband, had played in her life.” At the end the word heard at the kiss comes back to him: **“Generous tears filled Gabriel's eyes.”**

At the dance Gretta begged him to go to Galway, and he answered coldly: “You can go if you like.” The story's last paragraph: “The time had come for him to set out on his journey westward.” For a couple with this tail that is the main task: a journey to where the partner came from — to their town, their people, their past. Not erasing that past and not competing with it, but visiting it. Separating parents' voices from one's own. No longer measuring oneself against someone who is gone: the past has no future, it is easy to lose to it and impossible to win.

Joyce named this Death's minus too. Dublin seemed to him **“the centre of paralysis”**, and the aunts' dance had, year after year, never once “fallen flat”: the same guests, the same goose, the same speech. The danger of this tail is not an ending but the impossibility of one, when the past does not die and stands beside the couple like a third person.

Joyce himself lived this tail in its plus. His wife Nora was also from Galway, and there, before she met him, a young man she had loved died. Nora took her husband to his grave, and a year later Joyce wrote a poem in her voice: “Rain on Rahoon falls softly…” Someone else's past is neither erased nor defeated — it is given a place. The snow at the end of “The Dead” falls equally “upon all the living and the dead”, and keeps no one from going on.
